pass_a_gloss: But it is likely that someone, because of 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me', not having examined the intent of the Scripture, thinks that as it were the Saviour too was cowardly at the time of the passion; and he being cowardly, someone might say, who is noble for ever? First we shall inquire of those supposing these things about the Saviour whether he was less than the one saying: the Lord my illumination and my saviour, whom shall I fear; the Lord protector of my life, of whom shall I be cowardly; in the drawing near upon me of evil-doers to eat my fleshes, those afflicting me and my enemies themselves were weak and fell; if a camp is drawn up against me, my heart will not fear; if war rises against me, in this I will hope. Perhaps these words said in the prophet are of no other than the Saviour, fearing no one through the illumination from the Father and the salvation from him, and cowardly from nothing through the protection by which God protected him. His heart too in no way feared when the whole camp of Satan was drawn up against him; and his heart filled with sacred doctrines hoped upon God when war rose against him. It is not therefore of the same one both to say by cowardice 'Father, if possible, let this cup pass from me' and from courage to declare 'if a camp is drawn up against me, my heart will not fear'. Lest then something escape us in the place, you will also attend to the demonstrative of the cup said among the three. For Matthew wrote the Lord saying 'Father, if possible, let this cup pass from me', Luke 'Father, if you will, carry this cup away from me', Mark 'Abba Father, all things possible to you; carry this cup away from me'. See therefore if you can, every martyrdom accomplished by an exodus on whatever pretext being called a cup, say that the one saying 'let this cup pass from me' did not decline the genus of martyrdom (for he would have said 'let the cup pass from me') but perhaps this species. And attend whether possibly the Saviour, looking into the species, so that I may name them thus, of the cups and to the things that would come through each, and grasping with a certain deepest wisdom the differences, declines this species of exodus of martyrdom, but perhaps asks another heavier one secretly, so that something more universal and reaching to more, a benefaction, be accomplished through another cup; which was not yet the will of the Father to come about, he managing affairs by way and order more wisely than the wish of the Son and than what the Saviour saw. Clearly in Psalms the 'cup' of 'salvation' is the death of the martyrs. Therefore to 'I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord' is added 'precious before the Lord the death of his holy ones'. 'Precious' therefore comes upon us 'death', if we are holy to God and not unworthy, not to die the common, so that I may name it, and idle-of-godliness death, but some select one, the one through Christianity and piety and holiness.
pass_b_english: But perhaps someone, because of the words “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and without having looked closely at what Scripture means, will think that the Saviour too, as it were, was afraid at the time of his passion. And if he was afraid, someone might say, who is ever brave? But first we will ask those who suppose this about the Saviour whether he was less than the one who says: “The Lord is my light and my Saviour; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers drew near me to eat my flesh, those who afflict me and my enemies themselves grew weak and fell. If an army sets itself in array against me, my heart will not fear; if war rises up against me, in this I will hope” (Psalm 27:1-3).

Perhaps these words spoken in the prophet belong to no one else than the Saviour, who because of the light from the Father and the salvation from him feared no one, and because of the protection with which God shielded him was afraid of nothing. His heart did not fear at all when the whole army of Satan was set in array against him, and his heart, filled with holy teachings, hoped in God when war rose up against him. So it does not belong to the same person to say from cowardice, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” and to declare from courage, “If an army sets itself in array against me, my heart will not fear.”

Then let nothing in the passage escape us, and you will notice the word “this”, pointing to the cup, in all three. Matthew recorded the Lord as saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); Luke, “Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me” (Luke 22:42); and Mark, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup away from me” (Mark 14:36).

See, then, whether you can say this. Since every martyrdom, a departure brought about on whatever pretext, is called a cup, the one who said “Let this cup pass from me” was not refusing martyrdom as a kind (for then he would have said, “Let the cup pass from me”), but perhaps this particular form of it. And consider whether it may be that the Saviour, looking into the forms of the cups, if I may call them that, and into what would come about through each, and grasping their differences with a very deep wisdom, declined this form of departure by martyrdom and was quietly asking perhaps for another, heavier one, so that a more universal benefit, reaching more people, might be accomplished through another cup. That was not yet the Father's will to bring about, since he orders things by way and order more wisely than the Son's wish and than what the Saviour saw.

Clearly, in the Psalms the “cup” of “salvation” is the death of the martyrs. That is why “I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord” is followed by “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:13, 15). So a “precious” “death” comes to us if we are God's holy ones and not unworthy, so that we die not the common death, if I may call it so, which does nothing for godliness, but a chosen one: the death suffered for Christianity, godliness and holiness.

choices.choice: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 29). The old English replaced Origen's comparison of the three Gospels with a slash list ('let this pass from me' / 'bear away' / ...), dropped his question to those who think the Saviour was afraid, the reading of Psalm 27 as the Saviour's words, and the Psalm 116 close (alert item 9; mark/SOURCE_ISSUES.md item 1). The first lines of the source block (end of ch. 28) and its last lines (start of ch. 30) belong to those sections and are not translated here.
